subject: Efficently using samples from a Stan fit in a different model (a discrete index variable?)

messages.author: fb1667ba74f25458
messages.subject: Efficently using samples from a Stan fit in a different model (a discrete index variable?)
parts:
Hi,
I am currently trying to replicate a model of gene expression I found in the literature. The original model uses custom Metropolis/Gibbs sampler, but I am trying to implement it in Stan to gain efficiency (also the original code is not available and I like Stan). The model deals with time series of gene expression and uses a Gaussian process prior on unobservable series to estimate parameters defining a non-linear ordinary differential equation (ODE) of gene regulation. 

To be precise, there are two models used in succession: First, a transcription model that incorporates prior knowledge is fitted to estimate the (unobservable) levels of active protein over time. Every sample from the transcription model represents a possible time series of the estimated protein activity in 3 runs of the experiment (~100 time points each). Than a regulation model takes the posterior distribution (i.e. the actual samples) from the transcription model to infer ODE parameters of possible regulation of a target gene (repeatedly fitted for a large set of target genes). 

I have managed to build the transcription model and I have the basics of the regulation model (it allows only a single protein time series to be given as input).

Since the regulation model needs to be fitted about 10^5 times with different data (but same input from the transcription model), marginalizing over all (~1000) samples from the transcription model in every likelihood calculation is a no-go (computing the likelihood involves numerically solving an ODE for each input sample). In the original paper, the authors instead introduce a discrete variable that indexes the array of possible samples. This reduces likelihood calculation to only solving a single ODE. The index variable is then updated with Gibbs steps. I believe that one of the reasons why this actually works and is reasonably fast is that the posterior samples from the transcription model are quite similar - there are usually only few classes where within each class, the differences are just small perturbations.

Now I am not sure how to replicate this in Stan. I checked this group for past discussions of discrete variables, and it seems that it is possible to interleave NUTS steps with Gibbs steps with a reasonable amount of C++ code. The main drawbacks cited is that convergence may be problematic since the Gibbs steps are unlikely to be accepted as the current continuous parameters will probably provide low likelihood when the discrete parameters change. (here: https://groups.google.com/d/topic/stan-users/aWChDDz1YFI/discussion and here: https://groups.google.com/d/topic/stan-users/rHrxlhL46KQ/discussion ). This might not be an issue in my case, since the posterior samples are often quite similar (though not enough to let me squeeze them into a simple distribution).

Another idea I had is to make the index variable continuous by turning it into a simplex with an entry for each sample and use weighed averaged of the samples to construct a profile I will use. Since averaging arbitrary transcription samples could be misleading, I would force the average to be close to one of the samples by adding a strong prior equivalent to something like
max(my_simplex) ~ normal(1, 0.001)
(a smooth approximation to the max function could be some of the L_n norms for a sufficiently large n).

Do you have some intuition why either of the approaches could break badly? Or are there other ways to achieve my intended goal?

Also wanted to say that using Stan has been smooth sailing so far, you guys made a great software and the mailing list is a very helpful resource...

Thanks for any hints

Martin

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Efficently using samples from a Stan fit in a different model (a discrete index variable?)
parts:
We haven't experimented with mixing Gibbs or other discrete
samplers with MCMC. Better to marginalize them out in terms
of convergence. But that's not going to save you computation (but
then neither would Gibbs if you had to evaluate the various categorical
probabilities).

You can fit ODEs directly in Stan---we have stiff and non-stiff
solvers. GPs are hard to scale. It's hard to imagine a Gibbs
sampler or Metropolis could've succeeded in robust inference on
this task.

If you try to set up a very narrow prior, it introduces a ridge
into the posterior geometry that can be very hard to sample---you
wind up needing very small step sizes to deal with the poor conditioning
assuming the rest of your model's not on the same scale.

I think the main reason mixing discrete parameters with HMC is going
to fail is that changing the discrete parameters messes with the
adaptation for HMC, which is very sensitive.

- Bob

messages.author: fb1667ba74f25458
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Efficently using samples from a Stan fit in a different model (a discrete index variable?)
parts:
Hi,
thanks for the info. The paper is here: http://bmcsystbiol.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/1752-0509-6-53 but a better reference for the model is the supplementary material which has detailed description of both the model and the sampling procedure involved https://static-content.springer.com/esm/art%3A10.1186%2F1752-0509-6-53/MediaObjects/12918_2011_1007_MOESM1_ESM.pdf (kudos to the authors, most papers do not provide this level of detail). The relevant info is in chapters 2 & 4 of the supplementary material.

Bob: if I understand you correctly, you suggest that the only way to handle a distribution given by a set of samples is to either:
a) marginalize over all samples
b) avoid using the samples and use a different (approximate) approach
Is that correct?

I am aware of the built-in ODE solver, but in my case it messes up derivatives (using test_grad = TRUE gives errors on the order of 10^4 - I use RK45). At the same time the ODE can be analytically simplified to an integral that (given the nature of the data) can be accurately approximated with the trapezoid rule (implemented in Stan). This has so far been reasonably fast and accurate. I guess the problem with the built-in solver stems from the fact that the derivative is a function of the discretized protein profiles. This is OK with the trapezoid rule (I only use the time points where the protein profile is given), but RK45 needs to evaluate the derivative at arbitrary time points forcing me to interpolate the protein profile. The interpolation than probably messes up the derivatives (I need to use binary search to convert float time to the nearest int to perform a table lookup...).

I am however thinking whether there might be a good and general way to perform numerical integration in C++ with the Stan math library and somehow simplify the computation of gradients compared to the autodiff.

Thanks for quick replies, it is appreciated.

Martin

The relevant info is in chapters 2 & 4 of the supplementary material.
>
> Bob: if I understand you correctly, you suggest that the only way to handle a distribution given by a set of samples is to either:
Do you mean estimate the parameters of a distribution given a sample (set of draws)?

> a) marginalize over all samples
> b) avoid using the samples and use a different (approximate) approach
> Is that correct?

The usual approach is to either choose a general density function like
a Gaussian process or a parameteric density and fit it to the data
then use that.

I'm not sure how you want to make use of a set of draws.

> I am aware of the built-in ODE solver, but in my case it messes up derivatives (using test_grad = TRUE gives errors on the order of 10^4 - I use RK45).


> At the same time the ODE can be analytically simplified to an integral that (given the nature of the data) can be accurately approximated with the trapezoid rule (implemented in Stan). This has so far been reasonably fast and accurate. I guess the problem with the built-in solver stems from the fact that the derivative is a function of the discretized protein profiles. This is OK with the trapezoid rule (I only use the time points where the protein profile is given), but RK45 needs to evaluate the derivative at arbitrary time points forcing me to interpolate the protein profile. The interpolation than probably messes up the derivatives (I need to use binary search to convert float time to the nearest int to perform a table lookup...).

That's going to be a problem if the interpolation isn't smooth. This is
why we're considering just getting rid of the ability to even branch on
parameters---it's why we don't have a real to int rounding function.

- Bob
